justification_text:
At the time of this forecast, the asset appeared to be trading near the 329–330 level, which anchored my 1-day point estimate of 329.5. For the very near term, I leaned on mean-reversion tendencies and recent price momentum, expecting little drift over a single session. For the 1-week estimate of 331, I factored in a modest upward bias consistent with a slightly constructive short-term trend, while acknowledging that weekly moves tend to cluster around small net changes unless a catalyst intervenes. The 1-month estimate of 334 reflected a continuation of that mild bullish drift, extrapolating trend at a diminishing rate as uncertainty compounds over time and mean-reversion forces grow stronger relative to momentum.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each horizon. For one day, historical daily ranges suggested a tight band around ±8–9 points was appropriate, producing the 321–338 range. Over one week, volatility scales roughly with the square root of time, widening the interval to ±17 points. Over one month, the interval widens further to roughly ±32 points, reflecting both the mathematical accumulation of daily uncertainty and the possibility that the macro or fundamental backdrop shifts meaningfully. I also widened the tails slightly to account for the fat-tailed nature of financial returns, where extreme moves happen more frequently than a pure normal distribution would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a stronger-than-expected economic data release, a policy shift, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could rapidly push prices above the upper bound of any horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical deterioration, a financial stress event, or an unexpected hawkish policy surprise could send prices well below the lower bounds, particularly over the 1-month window where there is more time for such shocks to materialize and compound.

It is also worth noting that these intervals are probabilistic statements, not guarantees. The 90% confidence intervals mean I expected roughly a 1-in-10 chance of the outcome falling outside the stated range at each horizon. In practice, tail events in financial markets occur with somewhat higher frequency than classical models imply, so the true probability of an outside outcome may be closer to 15–20%. Anyone using this forecast should treat the bounds as approximate guides rather than hard limits, and update the view as new information becomes available.
